taxonomy.title: Esophagus — structural disease, inflammation and emergencies
taxonomy.scopeIn: Structural dysphagia, Zenker and other diverticula, EoE, strictures, foreign bodies, perforation and esophageal cancer staging/resection essentials.
taxonomy.scopeOut: Achalasia and motor physiology belong to esophagus-motility-achalasia. GERD, hiatal hernia and Barrett belong to esophagus-gerd-barrett-hiatal.
taxonomy.priorityReason: These focused diagnostic and emergency decisions complement the two larger foregut pathways.
researchAgenda: Sampling adequacy and EoE treatment sequence
Esophageal cancer staging and operative essentials
taxonomy.coverageReason: Live identities cover part of this scope. The research agenda flags breadth to check, and the topic worker must judge redundancy and question quality.
taxonomy.testingWeightBasis: Owner-directed editorial estimate of general-surgery testing relevance. No exam percentages or official blueprint weights are asserted.

question.reachedCurrentUpdate: Endoscopy shows rings and a fixed esophageal narrowing. Six biopsies from two levels show 30 eosinophils per high-power field; other causes have been excluded.
question.stem: Which treatment approach should be planned?

answerChoices.label: Dilation without anti-inflammatory treatment
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Dilation alone does not treat the underlying esophageal inflammation.

answerChoices.label: Fundoplication without esophageal dilation
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The returned findings support fibrostenotic eosinophilic esophagitis rather than an isolated reflux operation.

answerChoices.label: Sphincter injection without inflammation treatment
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Sphincter injection treats a different motility problem and does not address this narrowing or inflammation.

question.explanation: Refer for dilation of the symptomatic narrowing together with anti-inflammatory EoE care. Dilation does not replace treatment of the underlying inflammation.

agentReview.scope: Technical, editorial, source-traceability, and internal-consistency review; named clinician review remains required.

question.stem: Which investigation should be selected next for {patientName}'s swallowing symptoms?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: FEES report: first dyed-puree bolus
items.value: The image is obscured as she swallows. On the next clear view, the pyriform recesses are empty and no dyed material is visible in the laryngeal vestibule.

items.label: FEES report: later observation
items.value: Forty seconds later, with no additional bolus given, dyed material rises from below the postcricoid edge and pools in the left pyriform recess. She then coughs.

answerChoices.label: Fluoroscopic barium esophagram
answerChoices.rationale: The delayed return after visible clearance raises a proximal retention question. Fluoroscopic contrast evaluation investigates that anatomy; the observed point of return does not prove the entire source or a diverticulum.

answerChoices.label: Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD)
answerChoices.rationale: EGD is often the initial investigation for persistent esophageal dysphagia, but the observed delayed return makes initial contrast assessment of a suspected proximal pouch the better offered sequence. FEES and EGD are distinct examinations.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: EGD is often the initial investigation for persistent esophageal dysphagia, but the observed delayed return makes initial contrast assessment of a suspected proximal pouch the better offered sequence. FEES and EGD are distinct examinations.

answerChoices.label: High-resolution esophageal manometry
answerChoices.rationale: Manometry addresses motor physiology, but does not replace the initial structural assessment selected by this pattern.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Manometry addresses motor physiology, but does not replace the initial structural assessment selected by this pattern.

question.explanation: The report records visible clearance followed by return of the same material from below, rather than continuous observation throughout the swallow. Investigate a possible proximal retention process with a fluoroscopic barium swallow. The sequence does not prove a diverticulum or exclude events during the obscured view. FEES is not the EGD offered as an alternative; a pressure study answers a different question after structural assessment.

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Procedure
items.value: Esophagus traversed without a fixed narrowing; mucosa described as visually unremarkable.

items.value: Four fragments, gastric cardia: gastric mucosa without the reported abnormality.

items.label: Exposure during examination

items.label: Current course
items.value: Two further episodes with bread or meat; weight stable.

answerChoices.label: Esophageal biopsy: six samples from two levels
answerChoices.rationale: The visually normal examination and six total fragments do not establish adequate esophageal sampling: four fragments came from the stomach. The symptom pattern warrants the specified esophageal assessment before moving to physiology.

answerChoices.label: High-resolution esophageal manometry with provocative testing
answerChoices.rationale: This is a credible next step after an adequate structural assessment, but it would bypass the unresolved tissue assessment in this record.

answerChoices.label: Timed barium esophagram with a tablet challenge
answerChoices.rationale: This can investigate emptying or obstruction, but it does not complete the relevant mucosal sampling indicated by these records.

question.explanation: Six total fragments are not six esophageal biopsies from two levels. The gastric fragments do not supply the missing esophageal territory, and visual normality does not remove the sampling requirement in suspected eosinophilic esophagitis. Complete the supported tissue evaluation before selecting a subsequent physiologic test. The six/two criterion is directly recorded in the inherited ACG-supported claim; no new diagnostic eosinophil cutoff is introduced.

question.stem: Which first anatomic study best evaluates {patientName}'s swallowing symptoms?

answerChoices.label: Upper endoscopy
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Endoscopy is important in other dysphagia pathways but is not the preferred first anatomic study for this classic proximal-pouch presentation.

answerChoices.label: Neck ultrasound
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Ultrasound does not define the pharyngoesophageal lumen or retained contrast pouch.

answerChoices.label: Esophageal manometry
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Manometry evaluates motility rather than directly demonstrating the suspected proximal pouch anatomy.

question.stem: Which investigation best defines {patientName}'s suspected swallowing abnormality before treatment planning?

question.explanation: High cervical symptoms, gurgling and delayed return of recognizable food suggest a proximal pharyngoesophageal retaining pouch. question.stem: Which next investigation should {patientName} undergo?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Observed test meal
items.value: Initial oral transfer and first swallow were completed without cough. Five minutes later, after conversation, she brought back food from the meal and coughed.

items.label: Endoscopy report
items.value: The instrument passed through the upper esophagus and stomach; no obstructing mass or mucosal lesion was reported.

items.label: Prior swallowing images
items.value: Oral-transfer images saved; the lateral sequence ended as the bolus crossed the lower edge of the pharyngeal field. No retained-food compartment was characterized.

items.label: History
items.value: Symptoms are most noticeable with solid meals; she sometimes describes a wet sound in the neck before the return of food.

answerChoices.label: Contrast esophagram with pharyngoesophageal fluoroscopy
answerChoices.rationale: The delayed return of recognizable food after an initially completed swallow suggests a retained proximal compartment. Contrast fluoroscopy can define that anatomy rather than limit assessment to aspiration during the first swallow.

answerChoices.label: Fiberoptic endoscopic swallowing test
answerChoices.rationale: This is a credible aspiration assessment, but the timing and retained-food story require characterization of the proximal swallowing anatomy rather than another first-transfer assessment.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This is a credible aspiration assessment, but the timing and retained-food story require characterization of the proximal swallowing anatomy rather than another first-transfer assessment.

answerChoices.label: High-resolution esophageal manometry
answerChoices.rationale: Motor testing becomes a different next step after structural causes are adequately assessed; it does not first define the suspected proximal pouch.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Motor testing becomes a different next step after structural causes are adequately assessed; it does not first define the suspected proximal pouch.

question.explanation: The cough follows delayed return of retained food rather than the initial transfer alone. A normal traversed endoscopy does not characterize the dynamics of a suspected pharyngoesophageal pouch. A contrast swallow with appropriate cervical fluoroscopy is the selected anatomical investigation. The prior endoscopy is described accurately; omitted report content is not equated with an unexamined region.

question.stem: Which investigation should be selected next for {patientName}'s swallowing symptoms?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Endoscopic swallowing observation, first bolus
items.value: Dyed puree crosses the pharynx. The visible pharynx clears after swallowing, and no material enters the laryngeal vestibule during that swallow.

items.label: Same observation, 40 seconds later
items.value: Without another bolus, dyed material rises into view behind the arytenoids from below the postcricoid edge. She then coughs.

answerChoices.label: Fluoroscopic cervical esophagram
answerChoices.rationale: Initial transfer and clearance are followed by retrograde re-entry. That pattern raises an anatomic storage question near the pharyngoesophageal junction, for which a contrast swallow is an appropriate first study.

answerChoices.label: High-resolution esophageal manometry
answerChoices.rationale: A pressure study can address an esophageal motor question, but it does not first characterize the suspected proximal reservoir suggested by the return of material.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A pressure study can address an esophageal motor question, but it does not first characterize the suspected proximal reservoir suggested by the return of material.

answerChoices.label: Upper endoscopy (EGD)
answerChoices.rationale: Direct endoscopy is a common first test for ordinary esophageal dysphagia. Here the delayed retrograde material after initial pharyngeal clearance makes proximal anatomy the first question to characterize by contrast.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Direct endoscopy is a common first test for ordinary esophageal dysphagia. Here the delayed retrograde material after initial pharyngeal clearance makes proximal anatomy the first question to characterize by contrast.

question.explanation: The cough is delayed: the initial bolus clears, then material returns from below without another swallow. This should raise concern for a proximal reservoir rather than simply failed transfer into the pharynx. Fluoroscopic contrast assessment can characterize that anatomy before a pressure-based or direct-inspection pathway. The constructed observation suggests a pouch; it does not prove Zenker diverticulum or establish a new diagnostic accuracy rule.

question.stem: Which investigation best completes {patientName}'s assessment before the negative endoscopy is accepted as excluding an esophageal inflammatory cause?

answerChoices.label: Esophagoscopy with multilevel esophageal biopsy
answerChoices.rationale: The container distribution does not provide adequate esophageal sampling for the represented clinical suspicion.

answerChoices.label: High-resolution esophageal manometry
answerChoices.rationale: A motility study answers a different question and does not correct inadequate mucosal sampling.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: A motility study answers a different question and does not correct inadequate mucosal sampling.

answerChoices.label: Ambulatory esophageal pH-impedance monitoring
answerChoices.rationale: This assesses reflux exposure rather than completing tissue assessment for the represented inflammatory pattern.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This assesses reflux exposure rather than completing tissue assessment for the represented inflammatory pattern.

question.explanation: Symptoms and food impactions warrant consideration of eosinophilic esophagitis despite a visually normal examination. The biopsy containers include stomach and only two distal esophageal fragments. Appropriate assessment includes at least six esophageal biopsies from at least two levels, interpreted with symptoms and exclusion of other causes. The prior negative fragments remain valid findings within their sampling scope.

question.stem: Which plan best reconciles {patientName}'s mechanical response and current treatment record?

answerChoices.label: Restore swallowed budesonide with scheduled specialist review
answerChoices.rationale: Dilation relieves narrowing but does not replace treatment of the underlying inflammation.

answerChoices.label: Stop swallowed budesonide and follow swallowing symptoms
answerChoices.rationale: Symptom relief after a mechanical intervention does not establish control of the persistent inflammation.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Symptom relief after a mechanical intervention does not establish control of the persistent inflammation.

answerChoices.label: Stop swallowed budesonide and arrange another dilation
answerChoices.rationale: Repeated mechanical treatment does not substitute for inflammatory control, and no current obstructive symptom is represented.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Repeated mechanical treatment does not substitute for inflammatory control, and no current obstructive symptom is represented.

question.explanation: The improved swallowing demonstrates a mechanical response. The persistent biopsy findings concern a separate inflammatory process. The omitted component should be reconciled with the treating gastroenterology team rather than inferred to be unnecessary. Budesonide is the patient's previously selected therapy, not a claim that it is universally superior to other anti-inflammatory strategies.

question.stem: Which next treatment best addresses {patientName}'s residual disease?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Before dilation
items.value: Food-sticking episodes; rings and an esophageal narrowing. Multilevel biopsies established eosinophilic esophagitis.

items.label: Treatment record
items.value: Prescribed proton-pump inhibitor taken throughout the subsequent treatment period; dilation performed during that period.

items.label: Follow-up endoscopy
items.value: The endoscope passes the treated segment without resistance. Longitudinal furrows remain.

items.label: Follow-up biopsy
items.value: Both sampled levels contain numerous intraepithelial eosinophils with epithelial injury, similar to the pretreatment samples.

items.label: Symptoms
items.value: Food sticking fell from several episodes weekly to one episode over the last month.

answerChoices.label: Add swallowed budesonide to the disease-control plan
answerChoices.rationale: The mechanical response did not produce a corresponding tissue response during the established PPI treatment. Anti-inflammatory treatment remains needed; the supported plan separates that target from repeat dilation.

answerChoices.rationale: This targets the component that has improved, while the residual biopsy abnormality is not treated by dilation.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This targets the component that has improved, while the residual biopsy abnormality is not treated by dilation.

answerChoices.label: Continue the same PPI regimen without another disease-control change
answerChoices.rationale: The record shows similar inflammatory findings during that treatment, despite better swallowing after the mechanical intervention.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The record shows similar inflammatory findings during that treatment, despite better swallowing after the mechanical intervention.

question.explanation: Dilation improved passage, but the multilevel tissue findings remained abnormal during the documented PPI course. Mechanical relief does not substitute for anti-inflammatory care in fibrostenotic EoE. Adding a swallowed topical anti-inflammatory treatment is the selected offered plan rather than redilating the now-traversable segment or inferring tissue control from symptom relief. This item does not rank steroid preparations or prescribe a dose or universal treatment duration.

question.stem: Which removal pathway best fits {patientName}'s retained esophageal object?

answerChoices.label: Emergent therapeutic esophagoscopy for extraction
answerChoices.rationale: Liquid passage does not remove the injury risk of a retained sharp esophageal object.

answerChoices.label: Short-interval observation with repeat plain films
answerChoices.rationale: Negative films and liquid passage do not establish safe passage of the confirmed sharp object.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Negative films and liquid passage do not establish safe passage of the confirmed sharp object.

answerChoices.label: Immediate open operative extraction
answerChoices.rationale: No complication or circumstance requiring an initial operation has been supplied; therapeutic endoscopy is the initial removal approach.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: No complication or circumstance requiring an initial operation has been supplied; therapeutic endoscopy is the initial removal approach.

question.explanation: A sharp object in the esophagus can injure the wall even when it does not completely obstruct the lumen. Confirmed retention therefore requires emergent therapeutic removal. With no represented indication for an initial operation, endoscopy is the initial approach. A negative plain film did not settle the earlier retained-bone question.

items.label: Plain neck/chest films

answerChoices.label: Therapeutic endoscopic extraction now
answerChoices.rationale: The CT localizes a retained sharp object in the esophagus. Neither liquid passage nor the radiograph result removes the injury risk; the supplied findings support initial therapeutic endoscopy.

answerChoices.rationale: This pursues an additional leak study before the initial treatment despite the CT showing the retained target without the represented complication findings.

question.stem: Which biopsy plan should be used during {patientName}'s current endoscopy?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed teaching record; fictional patient observations

items.label: Earlier specimen containers
items.value: Three fragments labeled gastric cardia and three labeled gastroesophageal junction; all contain gastric-type mucosa.

items.label: Current examination
items.value: The esophageal lumen is patent. Subtle concentric rings extend above the junction; the stomach has no focal lesion. The lumen contains no impacted food bolus.

answerChoices.label: Six biopsies across proximal and distal esophagus
answerChoices.rationale: The earlier gastric-type fragments did not represent the symptomatic esophageal territory. Suspected EoE requires adequate biopsies from at least two esophageal levels.

answerChoices.label: Six biopsies across junction and gastric cardia
answerChoices.rationale: Repeating the earlier junction/cardia sampling does not provide the required multilevel esophageal evaluation.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Repeating the earlier junction/cardia sampling does not provide the required multilevel esophageal evaluation.

answerChoices.label: Six biopsies across antrum and gastric body
answerChoices.rationale: Gastric sampling does not resolve a suspected esophageal mucosal process producing this history.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Gastric sampling does not resolve a suspected esophageal mucosal process producing this history.

question.explanation: Six fragments are not an adequate negative esophageal evaluation if they all represent gastric-type tissue. Recurrent solid-food symptoms and rings warrant the appropriate esophageal biopsy strategy: at least six biopsies from at least two esophageal levels. Endoscopic appearance does not replace tissue evaluation. No current impaction, dilation decision or drug regimen is added.

question.stem: Which biopsy plan should be used before completing {patientName}’s examination?

exhibit.caption: Original constructed clinical record; fictional observations

items.label: Extraction site
items.value: A short patch in the distal esophagus is abraded where the bolus was lodged. There is no irregular mass, deep defect or fixed focal narrowing.

items.label: Remaining esophagus
items.value: Longitudinal grooves and fine circular ridges extend through the middle and proximal esophagus; the mucosa there has not been contacted by the extraction device.

items.label: Medication record
items.value: She was not taking a proton-pump inhibitor before this procedure.

answerChoices.label: Multilevel esophageal samples away from the extraction patch
answerChoices.rationale: Distributed sampling can identify the process underlying impaction while avoiding mechanically irritated tissue that confounds interpretation.

answerChoices.label: Directed esophageal biopsies of the extraction patch
answerChoices.rationale: This concentrates tissue at the mechanical injury and under-samples the distributed process.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: This concentrates tissue at the mechanical injury and under-samples the distributed process.

answerChoices.label: Esophageal biopsies after proton-pump inhibitor treatment
answerChoices.rationale: Treatment before sampling can mask the underlying histology. Uninjured sites can be sampled now.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Treatment before sampling can mask the underlying histology. Uninjured sites can be sampled now.

question.explanation: The grooves and ridges beyond the extraction site suggest a distributed esophageal process. The focal abrasion is also a mechanical sampling confounder. Obtain distributed distal and middle/proximal specimens away from that patch now. Do not treat an abrasion as the diagnostic target or start a potentially masking treatment before obtaining suitable tissue.

nodes.task: Which investigation should {patientName} undergo next to establish the cause of her persistent dysphagia?

choices.label: High-resolution esophageal manometry
choices.rationale: Pressure testing does not first characterize or sample the irregular lesion.
choices.temptation: Treat a traversable lumen as a completed structural assessment.
choices.correctUnder: Persistent dysphagia after adequate structural and mucosal assessment.

choices.label: Upper endoscopy with directed esophageal biopsies
choices.rationale: Direct inspection and tissue are needed to establish the cause of this irregular narrowing.
choices.temptation: Appropriate structural interpretation.
choices.correctUnder: An uncharacterized irregular mucosal/structural lesion.

choices.label: Endoscopic ultrasound of the esophageal wall
choices.rationale: EUS may help a later unresolved wall lesion, but initial mucosal assessment has not occurred.
choices.temptation: Choose deeper staging before initial lesion characterization.
choices.correctUnder: Suspicious narrowing persists after negative directed biopsies and cross-sectional assessment.

nodes.explanation: The available record does not establish inspection or tissue assessment of the imaged distal narrowing. Upper endoscopy with directed sampling addresses that gap before a physiologic diagnosis is assumed.

candidateCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 61-year-old woman, attends clinic after discharge. The founder reviews outside-hospital records of an esophageal injury during diagnostic endoscopy.

nodes.objective: Choose primary repair when a free thoracic leak has viable reparable tissue.
nodes.currentUpdate: Later records show fever, increasing pleural fluid and contrast entering the right chest. At exploration, the defect was focal. Its edges bled after debridement, adjacent esophagus was healthy and the edges approximated without tension. Pleural contamination was drained.
nodes.task: Which operative reconstruction best fit {patientName}’s findings at exploration?

choices.label: Esophagectomy with cervical esophagostomy and feeding access
choices.rationale: The supplied viable focal injury does not require removal of a destroyed or irreparable segment.
choices.temptation: Let contamination severity alone dictate organ removal.
choices.correctUnder: Extensive necrosis or irreparable diseased tissue.

choices.label: Esophageal diversion with decompression and feeding access
choices.rationale: Diversion is an option when primary repair cannot safely be achieved.
choices.temptation: Assume deterioration after observation eliminates repairability.
choices.correctUnder: A defect not safely closable in its actual tissue context.

choices.label: Reinforced primary esophageal closure with feeding access
choices.rationale: Viable healthy edges and tension-free approximation support repair with drainage and nutrition.
choices.temptation: Appropriate reconstruction based on acquired tissue findings.
choices.correctUnder: The supplied focal reparable defect after debridement and drainage.

nodes.explanation: The new free leak required source control. Viable healthy tissue permitting tension-free closure supports reinforced primary repair rather than automatic diversion or resection. Drainage and nutrition remain part of the operative care.
nodes.identityReason: A consequential meaning absent from the assigned scored concepts; no historical card is reassigned.

authorGate.coverTheKey: All options are reconstructions after drainage, so the key is not the only source-control plan. Each has feeding access and similar length. Raw edge findings replace the conclusion “repairable.”
authorGate.decisionStage: One operative reconstruction after exploration.
authorGate.interpret: Interpret viability, adjacent tissue and closure tension rather than contamination alone.
authorGate.apply: Preserve the esophagus with reinforced closure in the supplied context.
authorGate.difficultyReason: Resection is plausible for a severe free leak, but the operative tissue findings distinguish this injury.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Focal defect, bleeding viable edges, healthy adjacent tissue and tension-free approximation.
authorGate.counterfactual: Extensive necrosis or destructive disease preventing closure could support resection.
authorGate.deletionTest: Without the operative tissue findings reconstruction cannot be fairly ranked.
authorGate.sequenceAudit: Earlier conservative feedback gives no reconstruction answer; actual deterioration and new operative data change the decision.
authorGate.remainingRisk: Single direct guideline; no universal buttress, incision or antibiotic regimen.

candidateCases.name: Rene Evans
candidateCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 44-year-old man, attends clinic after an outside hospitalization for accidental caustic ingestion. The founder reviews initial injury and later swallowing records.

nodes.objective: Recognize full-thickness caustic injury despite stable pressure and absent free gas.
nodes.currentUpdate: The hospital CT used intravenous contrast with adequate enhancement of the nearby vessels. A thoracic esophageal segment showed no enhancement through its full wall thickness, with adjacent fluid. No free gas was present. {patientName} was normotensive without vasopressors.
nodes.task: Which initial hospital treatment pathway best fit {patientName}’s CT findings?

choices.label: Emergency exploration and removal of nonviable tissue
choices.rationale: Absent full-wall enhancement on an adequate study raises concern for transmural necrosis requiring emergency surgical treatment.
choices.temptation: Appropriate interpretation of wall perfusion.
choices.correctUnder: The supplied adequate CT with full-thickness nonenhancement.

choices.label: Endoscopic grading before deciding whether to operate
choices.rationale: Endoscopy may help equivocal or unavailable CT, but should not delay action on convincing full-thickness necrosis findings.
choices.temptation: Require mucosal grading before acting on deeper wall nonviability.
choices.correctUnder: Unavailable or contraindicated CT, or uncertain interpretation requiring further assessment.

choices.label: Monitored nonoperative care with serial clinical assessment
choices.rationale: Normal pressure and no free gas do not establish wall viability.
choices.temptation: Equate absence of perforation or shock with absence of full-thickness injury.
choices.correctUnder: Adequately enhancing wall without transmural necrosis or another operative indication.

nodes.explanation: An adequate contrast study can reveal wall nonviability before free perforation or shock. Full-thickness nonenhancement is the decisive finding here; it differs from a viable inflamed wall that may receive monitored nonoperative care.
nodes.identityReason: A consequential meaning absent from the assigned scored concepts; no historical card is reassigned.

authorGate.coverTheKey: No necrosis diagnosis appears before the choice. Vessel enhancement is necessary acquisition context. All alternatives are initial management pathways; the key is not padded with shared care.
authorGate.decisionStage: One initial hospital pathway after CT.
authorGate.interpret: Recognize absent full-thickness perfusion on an adequate contrast study despite absent free gas.
authorGate.apply: Select emergency surgical assessment/treatment instead of awaiting a mucosal grade or circulatory collapse.
authorGate.difficultyReason: Stable hemodynamics make observation tempting despite the deeper-wall warning.
authorGate.decidingObservation: The full wall does not enhance although the contrast study is technically adequate.
authorGate.counterfactual: Enhancement throughout the wall without full-thickness necrosis could support monitored nonoperative care.
authorGate.deletionTest: Deleting technical adequacy creates an artifact alternative; deleting wall perfusion removes the surgical discriminator.
authorGate.sequenceAudit: Later healed stricture data are withheld; no immediate dilation through injured tissue is implied.
authorGate.remainingRisk: One direct low-certainty guideline. Exact resection extent and reconstruction are not determined by this summary.

candidateCases.name: Rene Evans
candidateCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 44-year-old man, attends clinic for recurrent solid-food dysphagia after outside treatment and reconstruction for a caustic injury. The founder reviews the operative and swallowing records.

nodes.objective: Select dilation guidance for long angulated post-caustic narrowing.
nodes.currentUpdate: The hospital operation removed the nonviable mid and distal thoracic esophagus. A later gastric pull-up was joined to the retained proximal native esophagus. Current contrast imaging shows a long angulated narrowing and two additional short stenoses within that native segment above the anastomosis. The anastomosis and gastric conduit are patent. The standard endoscope stops at the first narrowing. Liquids pass, directed specimens are benign and no dilation has yet been attempted.
nodes.task: Which next procedure best fits {patientName}’s current reconstructed anatomy?

choices.label: Wire-guided balloon dilation with fluoroscopic guidance
choices.rationale: The long, angulated, multiple postcaustic narrowings and inability to traverse them favor fluoroscopic control of wire and balloon positioning.
choices.temptation: Use the actual residual native anatomy to choose guidance.
choices.correctUnder: A high-risk postcaustic stricture that is long, angulated, multiple or nontraversable.

choices.label: Wire-guided balloon dilation without fluoroscopic guidance
choices.rationale: A guidewire does not remove the additional value of fluoroscopy in this high-risk nontraversable multilevel anatomy.
choices.temptation: Assume that wire guidance makes direct endoscopic visualization sufficient for every stricture.
choices.correctUnder: A short, straight, traversable uncomplicated stricture with secure endoscopic orientation.

choices.label: Temporary placement of a fully covered esophageal stent
choices.rationale: Temporary stenting is a selected rescue strategy for refractory benign strictures. This native segment has not yet undergone a course of guided dilation.
choices.temptation: Choose durable luminal support immediately because several segments are narrowed.
choices.correctUnder: A proven benign refractory stricture after appropriate dilation attempts.

nodes.explanation: The obstructing lesions remain in native esophagus above a patent reconstruction. Their length, angulation, multiplicity and nontraversability make fluoroscopic guidance important during dilation. Both dilation options use a wire, so the question turns on the additional guidance required by this anatomy. A covered stent is a later option for selected refractory disease.
nodes.identityReason: Version 2 retains the exact prior concept ID and its scored meaning. The revised observations, options and wording address independent review. Prior definitions, reviewed v1 objects and any history remain on their original identities.

authorGate.coverTheKey: Specified what was removed, what native esophagus remains and where the narrowing lies relative to the anastomosis and conduit. Both balloon options now use a wire and differ explicitly in fluoroscopic guidance.
authorGate.decisionStage: One next procedural plan for established benign symptomatic postcaustic narrowing.
authorGate.interpret: Localize obstruction to retained native esophagus and recognize a high-risk complex stricture from its geometry and nontraversability.
authorGate.apply: Select fluoroscopic guidance during dilation and rank initial stenting below an appropriate dilation course.
authorGate.difficultyReason: A wire-guided endoscopic balloon is a credible proposal. The learner must decide when the wire alone does not address the added positioning risk of complex anatomy.
authorGate.decidingObservation: The residual native esophagus contains long angulated multilevel narrowings that the standard endoscope cannot traverse.
authorGate.counterfactual: With one short straight narrowing that the endoscope could traverse, wire-guided balloon dilation without fluoroscopy would become reasonable.
authorGate.deletionTest: Removing the location of the anastomosis recreates the prior anatomy ambiguity. Removing the complexity and nontraversability eliminates the reason to favor fluoroscopy.
authorGate.sequenceAudit: Standalone later follow-up version states the complete operative history. The original acute caustic PASS is split out and retains all exact reviewed wording.
authorGate.remainingRisk: BSG supplies the direct guidance recommendation. The specific reconstructed anatomy is a labelled synthetic clinical construction and does not assert how often this course occurs.

candidateCases.name: Martha Ellis
candidateCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 78-year-old woman, attends clinic for persistent regurgitation and weight loss after a completed swallowing evaluation.

nodes.objective: Match symptomatic proximal-pouch treatment to access and anesthesia constraints.
nodes.currentUpdate: Video fluoroscopy shows a posterior pouch above the cricopharyngeus filling with food and returning it to the pharynx after the swallow; coughing follows. Prior cervical fusion prevents neck extension. A previous general anesthetic required prolonged ventilatory recovery in the setting of severe COPD.
nodes.task: Which established treatment approach best fits {patientName}’s pouch and procedural constraints?

choices.label: Rigid endoscopic stapled septum division
choices.rationale: Rigid exposure is limited by neck immobility and commonly requires general anesthesia.
choices.temptation: Choose the familiar stapled approach without considering exposure.
choices.correctUnder: Adequate rigid transoral exposure and acceptable anesthesia risk.

choices.label: Flexible endoscopic septum division
choices.rationale: Flexible treatment can address the symptomatic septum while avoiding the rigid neck-extension limitation.
choices.temptation: Appropriate integration of dynamic symptoms and access.
choices.correctUnder: A symptomatic pouch in this restricted-neck context after expert assessment.

choices.label: Open diverticulectomy with cricopharyngeal myotomy
choices.rationale: Open surgery is valid but adds procedural/anesthesia burden in this pulmonary-risk context.
choices.temptation: Assume inability to achieve rigid access requires open surgery.
choices.correctUnder: A supported reason that endoscopic treatment is unsuitable, or suspicious lesion requiring resection.

nodes.explanation: The study links pouch emptying to symptoms, while neck immobility makes rigid exposure unattractive. Flexible septum division is an established option that can avoid that access limitation. The actual anesthesia and procedure plan still requires specialist assessment.
nodes.identityReason: Procedure selection is a new consequential meaning, not a transferred layer-recall card.

authorGate.coverTheKey: All alternatives treat the same pouch/septum; irrelevant distal operations are removed. Neck and pulmonary constraints earn their role in approach selection rather than announcing an available service.
authorGate.decisionStage: One established procedure approach after dynamic diagnosis.
authorGate.interpret: Correlate delayed pouch return with symptoms and recognize a rigid-exposure limitation.
authorGate.apply: Choose the established flexible approach while accounting for greater procedural burden of alternatives.
authorGate.difficultyReason: Open surgery is plausible when rigid exposure appears impossible.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Neck immobility and significant ventilatory recovery history, with symptoms linked to the pouch.
authorGate.counterfactual: A suspicious focal lesion requiring resection or another supported endoscopic-unsuitability factor could favor an open approach.
authorGate.deletionTest: Removing neck/pulmonary constraints makes a universal approach ranking indefensible; removing symptom correlation risks treating an incidental pouch.
authorGate.sequenceAudit: Standalone management case, separate from both frozen N3 diagnostic versions.
authorGate.remainingRisk: Single 2020 guideline, weak/low-certainty flexible-first preference. No ranking against modern Z-POEM; clinician must confirm single-best fit.

candidateCases.name: Olivia Grant
candidateCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 56-year-old woman, attends clinic after biopsy confirmation of thoracic esophageal squamous carcinoma. The founder reviews completed outside staging before treatment planning.

nodes.objective: Change the oncologic treatment strategy when completed staging establishes multiple distant deposits despite a locally operable primary.
nodes.currentUpdate: The thoracic lesion does not contact the aorta or airway. CT and PET-CT also show several lesions in both liver lobes. A liver-core specimen contains squamous carcinoma matching the esophageal tumor on specialist pathology comparison. {patientName} remains active and the primary lesion is technically removable.
nodes.task: Which initial anticancer treatment best fits {patientName}’s completed staging?

choices.label: Esophagectomy with regional lymphadenectomy
choices.rationale: Resection of the technically removable primary does not address the demonstrated distant tumor distribution.
choices.temptation: Let local technical resectability override completed systemic staging.
choices.correctUnder: A resectable localized tumor in a patient selected for an operative treatment pathway.

choices.label: Definitive primary and regional chemoradiation
choices.rationale: A primary/regional definitive plan does not address the multiple biopsy-supported distant lesions.
choices.temptation: Favor a nonsurgical curative local treatment when the primary is operable.
choices.correctUnder: An appropriate nonmetastatic tumor selected for definitive chemoradiation.

choices.label: Systemic cytotoxic chemotherapy
choices.rationale: Systemic treatment addresses disease demonstrated outside the primary and regional nodal field. Drug and biomarker decisions require oncology assessment beyond this item.
choices.temptation: Prioritize the anatomic extent established by imaging and compared tissue.
choices.correctUnder: Esophageal carcinoma with confirmed distant disease that merits active systemic treatment.

nodes.explanation: Matching carcinoma in a liver-core specimen establishes distant involvement despite technical removability of the thoracic primary. Systemic therapy addresses that distribution. The exact systemic regimen and biomarker selection remain outside this question.
nodes.identityReason: Version 2 retains the exact prior concept ID and its scored meaning. The revised observations, options and wording address independent review. Prior definitions, reviewed v1 objects and any history remain on their original identities.

authorGate.coverTheKey: Removed the uniquely cautious selected-through-oncology label. All three labels name concrete treatment modalities with comparable oncologic scope.
authorGate.decisionStage: One initial anticancer treatment strategy after completed tissue-supported staging.
authorGate.interpret: Correlate the liver-core histology with the thoracic tumor and identify distant disease.
authorGate.apply: Choose systemic treatment despite the technical resectability of the primary.
authorGate.difficultyReason: Once the liver specimen is explicitly matched, systemic therapy follows directly. Removing tissue confirmation would create a staging-acquisition question with a different objective.
authorGate.decidingObservation: The liver-core carcinoma matches the esophageal primary and lesions occupy both liver lobes.
authorGate.counterfactual: Without distant disease, an appropriate nonmetastatic thoracic tumor could enter a definitive chemoradiation pathway.
authorGate.deletionTest: The matching liver-core result alone selects the only systemic modality. Local technical resectability supplies a distraction without a second consequential inference.
authorGate.sequenceAudit: Standalone item has no prior staging explanation. It remains separate from both preserved early-cancer PASS cases.
authorGate.remainingRisk: Parked after one attempt because the cue repair leaves elementary confirmed-metastatic treatment selection. No biomarker-dependent regimen has been invented to add difficulty.

candidateCases.name: Helen Ward
candidateCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 64-year-old woman, attends clinic to review pathology after endoscopic resection of superficial esophageal adenocarcinoma.

nodes.objective: Distinguish lateral mucosal clearance from high-risk invasive disease after endoscopic resection.
nodes.currentUpdate: The en bloc specimen shows well-differentiated intramucosal adenocarcinoma. The deep margin is clear and no submucosal or lymphovascular invasion is found. Neoplasia reaches one lateral mucosal edge. High-definition follow-up endoscopy shows a raised 8-mm focus centered on the fibrotic resection edge. The remaining Barrett mucosa is flat. A thoracic surgeon and an advanced endoscopist consider her fit for their respective procedures.
nodes.task: Which next treatment best fits {patientName}’s pathology and follow-up examination?

choices.label: Esophagectomy with regional lymphadenectomy
choices.rationale: The adverse finding is confined to a local mucosal edge. The specimen lacks the deeper invasion or lymphovascular involvement that would create a stronger reason for regional oncologic treatment.
choices.temptation: Treat every positive margin as the same risk category.
choices.correctUnder: Submucosal or lymphovascular invasion creating concern beyond the endoscopically treated mucosa.

choices.label: Endoscopic submucosal dissection of the visible focus
choices.rationale: A visible lesion requires resection for local clearance and tissue assessment. Its fibrotic scar location favors an advanced dissection approach.
choices.temptation: Integrate local-risk histology with the actual appearance and tissue plane at follow-up.
choices.correctUnder: A visible superficial lesion in a scarred resection area that can receive expert endoscopic treatment.

choices.label: Endoscopic radiofrequency ablation of the Barrett segment
choices.rationale: Field ablation can treat appropriate flat remaining Barrett epithelium after visible neoplasia has been resected. It would remove the chance to assess this raised focus in a resection specimen.
choices.temptation: Apply the usual Barrett eradication step before dealing with a visible abnormality.
choices.correctUnder: Appropriate flat residual Barrett epithelium after complete removal of visible neoplastic lesions.

nodes.explanation: A positive lateral mucosal edge with otherwise low-risk intramucosal histology creates a local treatment problem. The raised focus should be resected before field ablation. Its scarred location favors expert submucosal dissection. Deeper invasion or lymphovascular involvement would instead increase the importance of regional treatment.
nodes.identityReason: Version 2 retains the exact prior concept ID and its scored meaning. The revised observations, options and wording address independent review. Prior definitions, reviewed v1 objects and any history remain on their original identities.

authorGate.coverTheKey: Replaced vague re-treatment and judgmental surveillance wording with three specific treatment procedures. Added the scar location and expert procedural resources needed to justify the chosen technique.
authorGate.decisionStage: One next oncologic treatment after completed resection pathology and follow-up endoscopic inspection.
authorGate.interpret: Distinguish lateral mucosal persistence from high-risk deeper or lymphovascular invasion, then recognize that follow-up contains a visible lesion in a fibrotic scar.
authorGate.apply: Choose local endoscopic resection with an appropriate dissection technique before Barrett field ablation.
authorGate.difficultyReason: Both surgery for a positive margin and ablation for Barrett neoplasia are credible shortcuts. The resident must retain the risk compartment and treat the visible scar lesion before the flat field.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Neoplasia reaches a lateral mucosal edge and a raised focus remains in a fibrotic scar, while the deep margin and lymphovascular assessment are favorable.
authorGate.counterfactual: If complete local clearance were confirmed and follow-up showed only flat remaining Barrett epithelium, radiofrequency ablation of that field would become appropriate.
authorGate.deletionTest: Removing favorable deep and lymphovascular findings weakens the local-versus-regional distinction. Removing the visible scar focus makes field ablation potentially appropriate.
authorGate.sequenceAudit: Self-contained standalone case. The separate lymphovascular PASS is unchanged and supplies no prior feedback here.
authorGate.remainingRisk: ESGE 2023 favors ESD in scarred areas with low-certainty evidence and specialist expertise. This is a specific feasible option among the offered procedures, with no claim that every positive lateral margin requires ESD.

candidateCases.name: George Lane
candidateCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 67-year-old man, attends clinic after endoscopic removal of a small esophageal squamous carcinoma. He asks whether clear margins complete treatment.

nodes.objective: Select an oncologic resection referral after complete staging when high-risk submucosal and lymphatic invasion make endoscopic local clearance insufficient.
nodes.currentUpdate: The en bloc specimen has negative deep and lateral margins. Carcinoma extends deeply into the submucosa; tumor nests lie in endothelial-lined lymphatic spaces. Completed CT and PET-CT show no enlarged regional nodes or distant lesions. {patientName} remains active without a major cardiopulmonary limitation.
nodes.task: Which next treatment plan best fits {patientName}’s resection and completed staging findings?

choices.label: Refer for esophagectomy with regional lymphadenectomy
choices.rationale: Deep submucosal and lymphatic invasion make local margins insufficient to settle regional risk. In this fit patient after completed distant staging, oncologic resection referral addresses the supplied high-risk findings.
choices.temptation: Appropriate separation of local clearance from regional oncologic treatment.
choices.correctUnder: High-risk invasive histology in a fit patient without distant disease after specialist staging and selection.

choices.label: Repeat endoscopic resection of the healed local scar
choices.rationale: Another local resection does not evaluate the regional implication of vessel invasion when margins are clear.
choices.temptation: Treat every post-resection concern as local incompleteness.
choices.correctUnder: A visible local residual focus after a lateral-only clearance problem without high-risk invasion.

choices.label: Continue surveillance after endoscopic local clearance
choices.rationale: Negative margins and small CT nodes do not cancel vessel invasion.
choices.temptation: Use imaging node size and local margins as proof of complete oncologic treatment.
choices.correctUnder: A fully assessed curative low-risk resection after appropriate review.

nodes.explanation: Clear margins describe local removal. Deep submucosal invasion and tumor in lymphatic spaces raise a separate regional-risk concern despite nonenlarged CT nodes. After completed distant staging in this fit patient, referral for esophagectomy with regional lymphadenectomy is the supported offered treatment plan. This does not rank surgery against all possible definitive chemoradiation strategies.
nodes.identityReason: A consequential meaning absent from the assigned scored concepts; no historical card is reassigned.

authorGate.coverTheKey: The first key generically combined more staging with assessment of treatment while its foils were treatment plans. Repaired by supplying actual completed CT/PET staging and comparing a concrete named oncologic resection referral with specific local plans. Raw endothelial-space findings replace a named invasion conclusion.
authorGate.decisionStage: One next oncologic treatment plan after completed distant staging and resection pathology; no uniquely cautious information-gathering key.
authorGate.interpret: Recognize deep submucosal and lymphatic involvement and separate that regional-risk evidence from local margins or CT node size.
authorGate.apply: Refer for oncologic esophagectomy with regional lymphadenectomy rather than further local scar resection or surveillance of local clearance.
authorGate.difficultyReason: Clear margins and nonenlarged nodes tempt calling endoscopic resection complete treatment.
authorGate.decidingObservation: Deep submucosal invasion and tumor in lymphatic spaces despite clear margins, with no distant disease on completed staging and no major operative limitation.
authorGate.counterfactual: A fully assessed low-risk mucosal lesion without vessel invasion or other high-risk features could receive endoscopic surveillance after curative resection.
authorGate.deletionTest: The vessel observation changes management; negative margins and CT size are purposeful competing evidence.
authorGate.sequenceAudit: Standalone; no local-margin feedback is visible in this case.
authorGate.remainingRisk: One direct ESGE guideline supports consideration of additional oncologic therapy including surgery in selected fit high-risk patients. Surgery is the supported offered plan, not a universal mandate or a ranking against all chemoradiation strategies. Exact clinician review remains required.

candidateCases.name: Evelyn Stone
candidateCases.presentation: {patientName}, a 70-year-old woman, attends clinic to review removal planning for an outside-placed stent used for a benign post-resection esophageal stricture.

nodes.objective: Choose an endoscopic staged removal strategy for a partially covered stent embedded in benign tissue.
nodes.currentUpdate: Outside records show a stent with covering across its middle but exposed metal at both ends. At the planned removal endoscopy, tissue grows through the exposed proximal mesh and that end cannot be mobilized with the initial gentle grasp. Imaging shows no leak or migration. The original stricture samples show scar without neoplasia.
nodes.task: Which removal procedure best fits {patientName}’s acquired stent findings?

choices.label: Mobilize the embedded ends mechanically, then extract the stent
choices.rationale: Tissue ingrowth through uncovered mesh can prevent safe mobilization and raises injury risk during extraction.
choices.temptation: Treat a fixed embedded end like a routine removable fully covered device.
choices.correctUnder: A nonembedded removable device whose ends can be mobilized safely.

choices.label: Place a fully covered stent inside it, then remove both in stages
choices.rationale: An inner fully covered stent can compress the ingrown tissue and facilitate later removal of the embedded device.
choices.temptation: Recognize exposed-end embedding and select the staged stent-within-stent method.
choices.correctUnder: An embedded partially covered esophageal stent selected for specialist stent-within-stent removal.

choices.label: Expose the device surgically, then remove it through an esophagotomy
choices.rationale: Surgical rescue may be required when endoscopic removal is unsuccessful or unsafe. Evidence reviewed here does not establish this route as an equally characterized comparator.
choices.temptation: Escalate directly to a local operation after the endoscopic grasp fails.
choices.correctUnder: Specialist determination that endoscopic removal cannot be achieved safely.

nodes.explanation: Covering in the middle with exposed ends identifies a partially covered device; tissue ingrowth explains fixation. Stent-within-stent retrieval places a fully covered device inside it before staged removal. This recommendation does not by itself establish a difficult comparative ranking against all specialist extraction techniques.

authorGate.coverTheKey: Expanded coaxial into the actual inside placement and staged removal. Replaced radical resection with a local surgical rescue concept and specified a mechanical-release competitor.
authorGate.decisionStage: One specialist removal procedure for an embedded partially covered esophageal stent.
authorGate.interpret: Infer device type from its covering pattern and distinguish true mesh ingrowth from simple nonmigration.
authorGate.apply: Match embedding to the staged stent-within-stent strategy while considering the limits of other extraction routes.
authorGate.difficultyReason: The stent-within-stent recommendation is recognizable to an advanced endoscopist. The competing extraction routes lack sufficiently comparable verified evidence in this packet.
authorGate.decidingObservation: The exposed proximal mesh contains ingrown tissue and cannot be mobilized with the initial gentle grasp.
authorGate.counterfactual: If a fully covered device had freely mobile ends without tissue ingrowth, mechanical mobilization and extraction would become appropriate.
authorGate.deletionTest: Deleting the covering pattern and tissue behavior removes the actual device-embedding inference. Failed grasp by itself becomes a route-novelty cue.
authorGate.sequenceAudit: Standalone advanced procedural draft is retained only as a parked author attempt, outside current proposed question supply.

constructedObservationPolicy: Original fictional named patients, demographic observations and acquired records are constructed teaching data, not empirical rates, disease-selection weights or new clinical cutoffs. ownerApprovalsNeeded.closestCompetingAction: Continue surveillance after endoscopic local clearance

rankedConcepts.closestCredibleError: A negative film excludes injury; any leak requires resection; stability alone permits observation.
rankedConcepts.consequence: Missed contamination or unnecessary major resection.

rankedConcepts.testingWeightBasis: Qualitative editorial estimate of resident decision relevance; no proprietary exam corpus, exam percentage, observed correctness or official topic-frequency claim.

The 12 historical rewrite rows consolidate into three candidate rewrites. Kept, retired/replaced, parked and held historical records were noted but not re-reviewed. Author self-checks, keys and source claims were not treated as proof. independentReview.title: Reconstruction after deterioration to a free esophageal leak
fairness: Reinforced primary closure with feeding access is the best offered reconstruction when debridement leaves bleeding healthy edges that approximate without tension. Diversion/resection are competing responses to concern about tissue failure or severe contamination.

The learner must recognize that the new leak changes the need for source control, then assess the actual operative tissue rather than reflexively escalate to resection because observation failed. Healthy approximating edges are necessary operative findings, not inappropriate answer teaching.
No confident clinical inaccuracy identified. The explanation keeps drainage and nutritional support within the operative plan and does not invent a time cutoff that automatically prohibits repair.

Sequence: a contained injury can deteriorate into a free pleural leak; the earlier surveillance answer and this new reconstruction are not contradictory. The current update and task stand alone at exploration, with prior feedback not naming the repair.

independentReview.title: Caustic injury with full-thickness loss of wall enhancement
fairness: Emergency exploration and removal of nonviable tissue is the best offered pathway for the represented full-thickness nonenhancement on an adequately enhanced study. Waiting for free gas or hypotension would be a consequential error.

The learner must interpret absence of wall enhancement despite adequate vascular enhancement, then act despite reassuring hemodynamics and no free gas. Endoscopic grading and monitored care are credible alternatives for a different depth/viability assessment.
The stem supplies observations rather than the diagnosis 'necrosis'; that term appears only as a treatment implication in the option and in feedback. No strong wording-only shortcut identified.

No confident clinical inaccuracy identified, although precise CT interpretation and operative extent require clinician review; the item appropriately avoids dictating a specific resection from the limited record.

This is an important anatomical gap after the preceding necrosis/resection pathway.

Use a neutral next-procedure task if stenting remains offered, or make all options actual dilation strategies.
Describe mutually exclusive guidance approaches explicitly and have a clinician verify their ranking in the specified reconstructed anatomy; do not invent dilation increments or waiting intervals.

The resident must interpret the functional study as symptomatic pouch disease and apply access/anesthetic constraints to procedure selection. Naming the neck restriction is necessary patient-specific information, not a reason to delete the deciding finding.

answerChoices.label: Repeat upright chest radiography
answerChoices.rationale: Plain imaging can still miss a wall injury and does not define its extraesophageal extent.

answerChoices.label: Chest CT with esophageal contrast assessment
answerChoices.rationale: The trajectory after instrumentation warrants CT evaluation for a leak and surrounding contamination.

answerChoices.label: Fluoroscopic contrast esophagram
answerChoices.rationale: A selected esophagram can identify a leak, but CT better evaluates the associated thoracic extent needed in this dyspneic postprocedural context.

decisionNodes.stem: Which initial esophageal intervention plan best fit {patientName}’s CT and clinical findings?
decisionNodes.currentUpdate: CT that afternoon showed a small upper thoracic contrast pocket draining back into the lumen, with no pleural spill or distal obstruction. After initial fluids {patientName} was afebrile, normotensive without vasopressors and without worsening organ function. The procedure found no pre-existing esophageal disease. At the regional esophageal unit, oral intake was withheld and intravenous antimicrobials and nutrition support were begun.

answerChoices.label: Thoracoscopic primary repair with mediastinal drainage
answerChoices.rationale: Repair is appropriate for an uncontained or otherwise nonconservative injury; the current contained stable setting supports monitored nonoperative care.

answerChoices.label: Inpatient surveillance without an initial closure procedure
answerChoices.rationale: Early containment, minimal contamination, stability and expert monitoring support nonoperative care with reassessment.

answerChoices.label: Esophageal resection with cervical diversion
answerChoices.rationale: No destructive or unreparable diseased segment is represented.

decisionNodes.explanation: Containment, contamination and clinical trajectory determine this choice. Early limited disruption in a stable patient can receive closely monitored hospital nonoperative care when expert surveillance exists. Shared supportive treatment remains essential.

decisionNodes.stem: Which operative reconstruction best fit {patientName}’s findings at exploration?
decisionNodes.currentUpdate: Later records show fever, increasing pleural fluid and contrast entering the right chest. At exploration, the defect was focal. answerChoices.label: Esophagectomy with cervical esophagostomy and feeding access
answerChoices.rationale: The supplied viable focal injury does not require removal of a destroyed or irreparable segment.

answerChoices.label: Esophageal diversion with decompression and feeding access
answerChoices.rationale: Diversion is an option when primary repair cannot safely be achieved.

answerChoices.label: Reinforced primary esophageal closure with feeding access
answerChoices.rationale: Viable healthy edges and tension-free approximation support repair with drainage and nutrition.

claims.statement: Persistent obstructive swallowing symptoms require structural and mucosal assessment; endoscopy can inspect narrowing and obtain esophageal tissue.
claims.limitation: Choice depends on the clinical phase; suspected proximal pouch and acute perforation use different pathways.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed esophageal clinical context

claims.statement: A negative biopsy does not close a suspicious stricture evaluation; cross-sectional imaging or EUS and repeat biopsy can be needed when the clinical or endoscopic findings still suggest cancer.
claims.limitation: One direct guideline; low-certainty evidence. Preserve the negative result within the tissue actually sampled. No empirical false-negative percentage or mandatory sampling device.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed esophageal clinical context

claims.statement: Evaluation for EoE requires at least six esophageal biopsies spanning at least two levels, including when the mucosa appears unremarkable.
claims.limitation: Numeric sampling minimum directly verified; samples from stomach/cardial tissue do not satisfy esophageal territory. No biopsy count by itself diagnoses EoE.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed esophageal clinical context

claims.statement: Symptoms of esophageal dysfunction together with a peak biopsy count of at least 15 eosinophils per high-power field and assessment of competing causes support EoE.
claims.limitation: High-power-field area varies; use the pathology laboratory standard. Constructed counts are observations, not newly asserted probabilities.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed esophageal clinical context

claims.statement: Dilation treats EoE-associated narrowing and is used with continuing anti-inflammatory therapy rather than as a substitute for disease control.
claims.limitation: Medication and diet options can be valid; no universal budesonide-versus-PPI ranking, dose or failure interval is inferred.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed esophageal clinical context

claims.statement: Symptoms, endoscopic findings and esophageal histology contribute to treatment assessment; easier swallowing after dilation does not establish histologic remission.
claims.limitation: The case with histologic remission supplies actual adequate follow-up biopsies; treatment effects are not inferred from symptoms alone.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed esophageal clinical context

claims.statement: An empiric elimination diet is an EoE treatment option; currently available allergy tests should not determine the elimination foods for EoE.
claims.limitation: This concerns EoE, not management of immediate IgE-mediated anaphylaxis. A least-restrictive initial milk-elimination trial is supported; no universal superiority over medicines or more extensive diets.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed esophageal clinical context

claims.statement: Mechanical abrasion at a food-bolus impaction site can confound inflammatory histology, so suitable esophageal samples should come from other sites.
claims.limitation: Single adequate consensus publication for the precise trauma-site boundary. Does not justify ignoring a suspicious lesion at that site.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed esophageal clinical context

claims.statement: A stenosis or focal mucosal lesion suspicious for neoplasia at food-bolus endoscopy warrants targeted biopsy to assess malignancy.
claims.limitation: Original focal observations must support suspicion; ordinary extraction abrasions are a different target.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed esophageal clinical context

claims.statement: Some swallowed bones are poorly seen on radiographs; a negative film does not exclude a retained esophageal bone.
claims.limitation: No exact sensitivity or claim that all bones are radiolucent.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed esophageal clinical context

claims.statement: CT is appropriate when a swallowed foreign body may have caused perforation or another complication requiring intervention.
claims.limitation: Do not generalize to routine imaging before every uncomplicated nonbony food-bolus extraction.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed esophageal clinical context

claims.statement: A sharp-pointed object retained in the esophagus requires emergent therapeutic endoscopic removal even when the patient can handle saliva.
claims.limitation: Urgency is supported; no fixed gameplay wait or numerical clinical removal deadline is authored.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed esophageal clinical context

claims.statement: Failed retrieval, extraluminal migration, proximity to vital structures or perforation can require operative foreign-body management rather than further luminal extraction attempts.
claims.limitation: One direct guideline. Approach depends on object location, contamination and tissue viability; no universal incision or extraction protocol.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed esophageal clinical context

claims.statement: CT with appropriate contrast assessment can identify esophageal perforation and its extraesophageal extent; a normal chest radiograph does not exclude the injury.
claims.limitation: The exact CT protocol is determined by the hospital team; an aspiration-prone completely obstructed patient is a different oral-contrast context.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed esophageal clinical context

claims.statement: A stable patient with early, contained esophageal disruption, minimal contamination and expert surveillance may be managed nonoperatively in hospital.
claims.limitation: One adequate direct guideline, low-certainty evidence. This excludes uncontrolled sepsis, freely leaking contamination and unmonitored outpatient observation.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed esophageal clinical context

claims.statement: Nonoperative perforation care includes withholding oral intake, antimicrobial treatment and nutrition support with close reassessment and drainage of collections when indicated.
claims.limitation: Single guideline; exact antibiotic selection and duration are not settled and are not authored.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed esophageal clinical context

claims.statement: For a free thoracic perforation with viable reparable tissue, operative source control can include debridement, reinforced primary repair and adequate drainage.
claims.limitation: One direct primary guideline. Destruction, diseased esophagus or inability to repair changes the role of resection or diversion; no universal rule for every leak.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed esophageal clinical context

claims.statement: After adult caustic ingestion, loss of esophageal wall enhancement on contrast CT raises concern for full-thickness necrosis and can support emergency surgery.
claims.limitation: One direct guideline. A technically adequate contrast study and clinical assessment are necessary; normal vital signs and absence of free gas do not by themselves establish viable wall.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed esophageal clinical context

claims.statement: Long, angulated, multiple or caustic esophageal strictures are high-risk dilation contexts in which fluoroscopic guidance improves procedural control.
claims.limitation: One direct guideline, moderate-certainty guidance. No novel diameter increment, mandatory number of sessions or fixed post-injury timeline.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed esophageal clinical context

claims.statement: Selected refractory benign esophageal strictures can receive a temporary fully covered removable stent after other approaches fail; uncovered or partially covered stents can embed.
claims.limitation: Not first-line treatment for an ordinary untreated stricture. No claim that stenting always beats incision, further dilation or surgery; candidate assumes specialist selection for a removable stent.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed esophageal clinical context

claims.statement: Fluoroscopic contrast swallowing can demonstrate a proximal pharyngoesophageal pouch and its dynamic relationship to regurgitation or aspiration.
claims.limitation: Single direct guideline for the new mapping; existing frozen PASS retains its original independent evidence and approval history.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed esophageal clinical context

claims.statement: Flexible endoscopic septum division is an established option for symptomatic Zenker diverticulum and can avoid the neck-extension limitations of rigid endoscopy.
claims.limitation: One adequate direct guideline. Flexible-first preference is weak/low certainty; no universal superiority over open surgery and no ranking against modern Z-POEM.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed esophageal clinical context

claims.statement: Multiple biopsy-supported distant metastases from esophageal cancer generally call for a systemic oncologic treatment strategy rather than a definitive plan limited to the primary and regional nodes.
claims.limitation: One adequate accessible government professional evidence summary. Does not specify a drug regimen or rule out selected local palliation; the candidate has multiple hepatic deposits, not an oligometastatic exception.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with multiple confirmed hepatic deposits matching an esophageal squamous carcinoma.

claims.statement: A positive horizontal endoscopic-resection margin without submucosal invasion or other high-risk histology can be managed through local endoscopic surveillance or re-treatment.
claims.limitation: One direct society guideline. The candidate supplies visible residual local tissue, making re-treatment the offered local plan; this is not a general rule to observe all positive margins.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed esophageal clinical context

claims.statement: Lymphovascular invasion or deep submucosal invasion after endoscopic esophageal cancer resection makes local clearance insufficient; full staging and additional oncologic treatment, including surgical consideration in selected fit patients, are warranted.
claims.limitation: One direct society guideline. Additional treatment is selected through multidisciplinary clinical assessment; the candidate completes distant staging and selects a fit patient. No exact nodal probability, universal esophagectomy mandate or ranking against every chemoradiation strategy.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults in the explicitly constructed esophageal clinical context

claims.statement: An embedded partially covered esophageal metal stent can be removed using a fully covered stent placed inside it as a staged endoscopic technique.
claims.limitation: One directly verified society guideline recommendation 8. Exact device, dwell interval and operative escalation depend on specialist assessment; none is invented.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with a partially covered esophageal stent embedded at its uncovered ends without a complication requiring primary surgery.

questions.stem: Which tissue-acquisition procedure should {patientName} undergo next for this narrowing?

answerChoices.label: Repeat mucosal forceps biopsies of the narrowed segment
answerChoices.rationale: The documented samples already represent the intact surface at this site. Repeating the same surface acquisition leaves the wall process unresolved.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The documented samples already represent the intact surface at this site. Repeating the same surface acquisition leaves the wall process unresolved.

answerChoices.label: EUS-guided needle sampling of the thickened wall
answerChoices.rationale: Needle acquisition under ultrasound can reach the deeper wall compartment implicated by CT after representative mucosal samples are negative.

answerChoices.label: Diagnostic mucosal resection from the narrowed segment
answerChoices.rationale: There is no visible superficial lesion to delimit and resect. A mucosal resection does not reliably acquire the deeper wall process.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: There is no visible superficial lesion to delimit and resect. A mucosal resection does not reliably acquire the deeper wall process.

questions.explanation: The negative specimens represent the inspected mucosal surface. CT localizes the unresolved abnormality within the wall, so the next acquisition must reach that compartment. EUS-guided needle sampling can establish its nature. A newly identified superficial lesion would instead support targeted surface sampling or resection.

questions.stem: Which next plan best addresses {patientName}’s persistent solid-food dysphagia?

answerChoices.label: Replace budesonide with dupilumab and reassess swallowing
answerChoices.rationale: The tissue response does not support first attributing persistent symptoms to inflammatory treatment failure.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: The tissue response does not support first attributing persistent symptoms to inflammatory treatment failure.

answerChoices.label: Continue budesonide and arrange graded esophageal dilation
answerChoices.rationale: A fixed symptomatic narrowing persists despite tissue response; mechanical treatment complements ongoing inflammation control.

answerChoices.label: Continue budesonide and repeat endoscopic mucosal biopsies
answerChoices.rationale: Adequate follow-up tissue already documents inflammatory response; repeat sampling does not address the fixed obstruction.
answerChoices.distractorRationale: Adequate follow-up tissue already documents inflammatory response; repeat sampling does not address the fixed obstruction.

questions.explanation: The follow-up tissue and the lumen answer different questions. Continue disease-control treatment and plan graded dilation for the persistent fixed narrowing. Symptoms do not by themselves establish pharmacologic failure.

answerChoices.label: Contrast-enhanced CT of the neck and chest
answerChoices.rationale: New fever and spreading chest pain require assessment for an object and extraesophageal complications despite negative films.

answerChoices.distractorRationale: Repeating limited bone imaging does not adequately define the new complication concern.

answerChoices.distractorRationale: Endoscopy can evaluate luminal retention, but the new systemic/chest findings warrant complication assessment before instrumentation.

questions.explanation: A negative film does not exclude a retained bone. The new trajectory also raises an extraesophageal injury question. CT can define complications before choosing an extraction route.

questions.stem: Which investigation was most appropriate next for {patientName} at that hospital assessment?

answerChoices.label: Repeat upright chest radiography

answerChoices.distractorRationale: An unrevealing radiograph does not resolve the combination of persistent symptoms and new respiratory findings after instrumentation.

answerChoices.rationale: This study can identify a wall leak and define mediastinal or pleural gas and fluid while assessing the surrounding chest.

answerChoices.distractorRationale: Repeat luminal inspection has a selected role when imaging remains uncertain or immediate endoscopic treatment is planned. Initial diagnostic re-instrumentation may enlarge an injury and does not map the surrounding chest.
